case_studies.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.
case_studies.summary: This research shows that using a persistent state‑based deception system, powered by a local language model, can force attackers to spend more time and resources while keeping defender cost lower. They built an SSH honeypot that keeps each attacker’s view consistent with their past actions and measured a 63 % reduction in defender effort compared to a basic LLM decoy. It is directly relevant to IT infrastructure managers looking to improve cost‑effective deception.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage SSH or similar services, integrate a persistent state honeypot: 1) set up Cowrie with a local LLM; 2) configure the LLM to only render state, not store it; 3) monitor and adjust Deception Exchange Rate to keep defender costs under 63 % of a basic decoy.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel deception technique using LLMs in a honeypot context. It directly impacts security tooling and endpoint management by potentially reducing defender compute costs. However, the implementation is only demonstrated in a proof‑of‑concept with Cowrie, lacking widespread deployment or released code, limiting maturity. The monetisation potential is modest: IT engineers could integrate a similar approach, but immediate commercial use would require further development and testing. Overall, the paper offers moderate real‑world relevance but low maturity and modest monetisation prospects, yielding a borderline score of 30, so a low_signal flag is set.

case_studies.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
case_studies.abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.
case_studies.summary: PersonaFactory builds a pipeline that creates a huge synthetic persona bank and augments training dialogues with user personas to improve style and intent preservation in LLMs. The system produces 740,000 detailed personas and 1.24 million persona‑styled conversations across 85 languages, and shows that these enriched data help models match user style without losing intent. It is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a synthetic persona generation pipeline that could be used to augment training data for LLMs. However, it is primarily a research prototype with no demonstrated deployment in real IT infrastructure or SaaS tooling. The approach is relevant to data preparation for AI models, but it does not directly affect how IT engineers manage Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or cloud endpoints. The system appears built and tested, but it is not a ready-to‑deploy product. Commercial applicability within 90 days is uncertain, as the pipeline would need integration into existing data pipelines or LLM training workflows, which is non‑trivial. Overall impact and monetisation potential for typical IT engineers are limited.
